A round is one pass over a single commit of the campaign branch. Each time a fix lands, the branch gets a new tip, and the campaign starts a new round there.

- **During a round**, the engine runs every stage up to the current one at that tip, and waits for triage and the fixer to produce PRs for whatever fails.
- **When the fixes land**, the round ends and the next one starts at the new tip.

For this campaign:

- **Round 1, at `e425d88` (the original cut from master).** Push passed. Hourly failed on #4613 and #4869. It ended when #5158 (#4613's fix) merged into the branch at 22:02.
- **Round 2, at `38089ad` (after #5158 landed).** Push and hourly are both rerunning. Push reruns because a stage counts as passed only when every stage up to it is green at the same tip. If hourly fails again on #4869, round 2 waits for that fix, and its landing starts round 3.

The round number counts across the whole campaign; it doesn't restart at each stage. The engine pauses after eight rounds in one stage, so a fix cycle that never converges stops instead of looping.

The messages don't make this clear: "Round 2: dispatching push at 38089ad" doesn't say what started round 2. If you'd like, I'll reword them to carry the reason. For example:

- "New tip 38089ad (after #5158 landed), round 2: rerunning push and hourly"
- "Round 1 ended: merging #5158 into the branch"

I agree, at least for these two tests. The evidence argues against a four-hour job as well as the cost:

- **They don't finish at all.** On Linux, single-threaded with the repository's settings, neither test had started its first file after three hours; both were still building the analyzer for the 1,518-file corpus. David's Windows run failed at about four hours with no result. A job that takes longer than its own interval can't run every four hours without overlapping itself.
- **This isn't a scheduling question.** If a test can't finish in a CI job, moving it to a slower schedule doesn't fix it. The test is acting as a performance benchmark of the analyzer on the whole repository, not a correctness check.
- **The bounded controls already cover correctness.** The fixture-corpus test (252 files) finishes in a few minutes and stays in the regular tier under every plan.

**What I'd recommend instead:**
1. **Take the two full-crates tests out of scheduled CI entirely.** Make them opt-in, for example manual dispatch only or ignored by default, and keep the bounded controls in hourly. That's #5144 minus the new four-hourly workflow and its budget question. It also unblocks the campaign, because hourly passes once the tests leave it.
2. **Track the slowness as its own performance issue.** David's fixpoint change (whole-map copies per successor) shows there's real performance work here. When the full corpus can finish in a reasonable time, it can return as a nightly or weekly job with a measured budget.

**The catch:** this reverses David's explicit October 13 decision, and his "I am not approving the manual-only coverage change" comment on #5144. So it's your call, and you'd probably want to tell him first.

I mentioned single-threaded because my understanding is that's the case for our current test suite, right?

Mostly, with one distinction: each test is single-threaded inside, but the suite as a whole still runs in parallel.

- **Where it's set:** `.cargo/config.toml` (lines 4–5) puts `BIFROST_PARALLELISM = 1` and `RAYON_NUM_THREADS = 1` in the `[env]` of every Cargo-launched process, including `cargo test` and nextest. It was added in `cc0a1f626d` on 2026-08-25, "Cap Cargo-launched internal test parallelism". `force = false` means an environment variable set outside Cargo, for example in a workflow `env:`, takes precedence.
- **What that means:** nextest runs many test processes at once, roughly one per core, so each test's own analyzer parallelism is capped at one thread to avoid oversubscribing the machine. For thousands of small tests that's the right default.
- **Where it hurts:** a handful of huge whole-repository tests each get one core for an hour or more. Every hourly and nightly matrix leg inherits this, because those workflows don't override it. `pre-push-gate.sh` uses the same default. Only some perf/benchmark workflows set their own values: `benchmark.yml` and `usagebench-qualification.yml` use 2, the others use 1.

So your nightly category fits the existing setup: a separate job that runs only the slow real-world tests, with `BIFROST_PARALLELISM`/`RAYON_NUM_THREADS` set to the core count, and nothing else competing for the cores. Because of `force = false`, the job's `env:` overrides `.cargo/config.toml` without changing the default for everything else.

The survey agent is still enumerating every test with an extended limit, which ones walk whole-crate or whole-repository corpora, and which existing mechanisms could host the category. I'll report the counts when it finishes.

The category is smaller than it feels: three tests walk all of `crates/`, and only two of them are stuck single-threaded. Most of the other "extended runtime" changes are something else. Details are in the survey's [report](.mj/agents/655c6214e4137223a60654a7ab01bdf3/slow-tests.md).

**Whole-`crates/` corpus tests: 3**

| Test | Threading | Time limit |
|---|---|---|
| `partial_flow_differential::algorithm_differential_over_crates` | Single-threaded: a serial loop over files and procedures, plus the one-worker defaults | default 600 s; times out |
| `partial_flow_differential::host_differential_over_crates` | Same | default 600 s; times out |
| `semantic_ir_rows_round_trip_every_workspace_crate_source` | Already uses every CPU through its own worker threads | 1,800 s (raised in `a371a862f8`, October 8) |

One more scheduled test uses a real corpus: `issue_3006_release_zero_config` indexes the actual JDK `jmods`, and explicitly sets its child process to `BIFROST_PARALLELISM=1`.

**The other runtime extensions are a different category.** None of them involves a large corpus or a forced single thread:
- **JS watchdog** (120 → 240 s, then 60 s, then 240 s on Windows): a bounded generated fixture with an explicit four-thread pool.
- **GC and pack-installer retry bounds** raised to 120 s.
- **Benchmark child-process bounds** of 240 s. The benchmark test copies `testcode-java`, not the whole repository.
- **Windows/ARM job timeouts** raised from 60 to 120 minutes. Those cover the whole job, and the history blames cold builds and cache starvation.

The semantic-IR test is the only one whose per-test limit is above the 600-second default.

**On single-threading:**
- **Source:** the defaults in `.cargo/config.toml`. Bifrost's AGENTS.md (line 258) says it's to keep "per-test worker pools [from multiplying] nextest's concurrency".
- **No serialized suite:** there's no `--test-threads=1` and no serial test group, so the suite itself runs in parallel.
- **Important for your plan:** giving the partial-flow tests more threads through the environment won't help, because their loops over files are serial. They need a code change to run files in parallel, the way the semantic-IR test already does. Until then they use one core no matter what runner they're on.

**How tiers work today:**
- **One flag for both schedules:** a test marked `cfg_attr(not(scheduled_tests), ignore)` runs in both hourly and nightly, since both pass `--cfg scheduled_tests`. There's no separate nightly-only tier.
- **One precedent for selecting tests:** the property-stress job in `nightly.yml` (lines 185–249) picks ignored tests with a filter, and a slow tier can reuse that.

**How your tiers would map onto this:**
- **Nightly, multi-threaded, real-world:** take the three corpus tests, plus the JDK `jmods` test if you want it, out of `scheduled_tests` and mark them ignored. A separate nightly job runs only those, using the property-stress style of selection, with `BIFROST_PARALLELISM`/`RAYON_NUM_THREADS` set to the runner's core count. The two partial-flow tests also need their per-file loop parallelized; otherwise they gain nothing.
- **Every two hours:** from the hourly set, the only candidate is the semantic-IR round trip. It's already multi-threaded and within its 30-minute limit, so moving it out of hourly only saves cost. The partial-flow tests can't run at any frequency until they're parallelized or made faster.
- **#4869 and the campaign:** this plan would replace David's four-hourly job. Taking the two partial-flow tests out of the hourly suite is still the step that lets the campaign's hourly stage pass.
